name: otherworld-73-step-mutator-clk
author: Andreas Jansson
description: A drum machine for effects. Each clock pulse is a step, and each of the 11 steps holds one of four moves on the last quarter beat: a deep drawl two octaves down, a double repeat an octave down, a four-fold stutter at pitch or an eight-fold roll an octave up, forward on the left and backwards on the right. Every note you play mutates the step it lands on, there and then: the drawl snaps into a repeat, the repeat into a stutter, the stutter into a roll, and a roll collapses back into the drawl. The pattern remembers: it loops its rhythm while you rest and rewrites itself where you play, and eleven steps against your bars spread the changes around. A steady stream of notes lifts the whole pattern up the ladder until it collapses into the deep drawl and climbs again. Reach moves the replayed slice back onto the beat's own attack; Regen feeds the slices back in, so they get sliced again.
title: Step Mutator_clk

validation.scope: Native 32.768 kHz; inherited 16-bit delay model; software only, no hardware timing or fidelity claim.

name: otherworld-93-tesseract
author: Andreas Jansson
description: The sixteen corners of a tesseract are sixteen ways to replay a slice of what you just played: left or right, forwards or backwards, at pitch or an octave down, from two or four slices back. On every step the cube turns to a new corner, and you hear that corner on the left and the corner opposite it on the right, which is different in every way: a slice played forwards at pitch from close by on one side is answered by a slice reversed an octave down from further back on the other. As the cube turns, the pair walks a tour of all the corners, and the tour is a pattern that repeats: sixteen steps when it turns by one corner, eight, four, and at eight corners a step it flips straight to the opposite corner. Your notes spin it: each note speeds the turning up, so the tour gets shorter and wilder while you play, and when it passes half a turn a step it snaps still and starts spinning up again; rests let it slow down. No clock needed: Time is the time between steps, like the clock pulse of the _clk version, from 0.05 s to 2 s. Slices are as long as a step up to a quarter second; on slower steps each slice stays a quarter second long and the rest of the step is a rest. Turn sets how it turns on its own (0: it rests between notes), Spin how hard each note pushes it.
title: Tesseract

validation.scope: Native 32.768 kHz; inherited 16-bit delay model; software only, no hardware timing or fidelity claim.

name: otherworld-95-zenos-arrow
author: Andreas Jansson
description: Zeno's paradox on a beat you set. An arrow catches what you play the moment it is fired and plays it back an octave down and slowed to half speed, then again at pitch in half the time, then an octave up in a quarter of the time, two octaves up in an eighth, each repeat thrown to the other side: a ping-pong that accelerates and climbs and lands exactly on the step it was aimed at. The arrows themselves follow Zeno too: the phrase is 16 steps, and each arrow flies half of what is left, 8 steps, then 4, 2, 1 and a last quick one, so a slow, deep flight is followed by shorter and shorter ones until the phrase lands in a flurry, and the next long flight starts. There is no clock to patch: the Time knob is the step, one every 0.05 s to 2 s (300 bpm sixteenths to 30 bpm quarters), and the steps run on steadily by themselves, just as a clock patched into the clocked twin would. Your notes are the payload and choose the height: a loud note keeps halving up to the 30 ms limit, a soft one climbs a step or two, and a rest stays low and slow.
title: Zeno's Arrow

validation.scope: Native 32.768 kHz; inherited 16-bit delay model; software only, no hardware timing or fidelity claim.
